42.0.s.en: 1. Things of which one must not be ashamed

42.0.0.en: 1 Then shall thy shame be in its place, and thou shalt find favour before every man. But of these things be not thou ashamed, and accept no person to sin thereby: 2 of the law of the most High, and his covenant, and of judgment, that the ungodly be not justified; 3 of the reckoning of thy friend with strangers, and of dividing the inheritance among friends; 4 of exactness of balance and measure, and of gain, whether much or little; 5 and of indifferent selling among buyers, and of much correction of children, and of making the side of a wicked servant to bleed. 6 Sealing is best for a wicked wife. 7 And where many hands are, shut up; and when thou dividest, do it by number and weight; and in giving and receiving let all be in writing. 8 Be not ashamed to instruct the unwise and foolish, and the aged that contendeth with the young. Then shalt thou be truly instructed, and commended before all men living.

42.0.1.en: Do not be ashamed of the following things:

42.0.2.en: And do not let partiality lead you into sin [1].

42.1.0.en: There are five things which must be supported and not be ashamed of, and they are: 1. Holding fast to the law of the Most High and His covenant [2], and supporting the wronged man even if he is a pagan (Sir 4:9). 2. Sharing equally in the expenses of a journey and receiving what is due to one in an inheritance [3]. 3. Trading faithfully without greed [4]. 4. Behaving with propriety in work, as with the members of the household and the workers (slaves) [5]. 5. Behaving with exactness [6-8].

42.1.1.en: Of the law of the Most High and His covenant, and of justice, lest thou justify the wicked [2].

42.1.2.en: It is no wonder that Ben Sira opens the things of which the believer must not be ashamed, and which establish justice without partiality, with the law of the Most High and His covenant [2]. Some of the Jews who were attracted to Hellenistic philosophy were embarrassed to declare their faith in God and denied circumcision (1 Macc 1:15). They became ashamed in an unseemly way, fearing that those of the pagan Hellenistic culture, which prevailed in some societies at that time, would despise the Jewish Law and the covenant with God.

42.1.3.en: Some fathers and mothers discovered what is called the "generation gap" to a degree unprecedented among the Jews. The young sons were ashamed of the Law and the covenant. This led to a real catastrophe among the Jews in Judea. This is what moved the Maccabees to revolt against this situation, as is recorded in the books of the Maccabees and in the "Antiquities" of Flavius Josephus, the Jewish historian.

42.1.4.en: The Lord Christ gave a warning against such embarrassment, when He said: "Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels" (Mk 8:38). And the two statements [1, 2] agree with the teaching of the Apostle Paul: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek" (Rom 1:16). Something like this happened when the Apostle Paul preached among the Gentiles, and a dispute arose between the believers of Jewish origin and those of Gentile origin. So with all power the Apostle said: "I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ" (Rom 1:16).

42.2.0.en: And of contributing to the expenses of the work, or of companions on a journey, and of dividing the inheritance among friends [3].

42.2.1.en: After Ben Sira directed the believers toward the law of the Most High and the believers' entry into a covenant with God, he dealt with some practical matters that prevailed at that time. If the Law urges the believers to give more than to take, what is the position of the believer if he undertakes a work that benefits him and some of his brethren: should he be ashamed to ask them to contribute to the cost of the profitable work and to the expenses of the journey that were necessary to reach a gain from which many benefit? Ben Sira affirmed that there is no need to be ashamed of those who benefit from the work contributing to its expenses. As for the lawful inheritance, the believer should not be ashamed to take his share of the inheritance, for each person receives his right, but if someone wishes to give up his right or a share of it to his friends, this is counted a higher degree.

42.3.0.en: And of exactness in the balance and the measure, and of gain, whether much or little [4].

42.3.1.en: As for a work that a group did and which produced a profit or gain, great or small, no one should be ashamed to take his share of the profit, provided that this gain is not the result of tampering with the balance or the measure or the specifications.

42.4.0.en: And of profit in dealing with merchants, and of much correction of children, and of striking the ribs of the wicked servant until they bleed [5].

42.4.1.en: It is no shame for a man to practice trade and make a profit, nor to discipline children so that they behave in the house with order and proper arrangement. Truly the talk here about disciplining the wicked servant seems harsh, but it was an important matter in ancient societies that if wicked servants were left without discipline, they committed terrible crimes and ran away.

42.5.0.en: Locking up wealth is good where the wife is not trustworthy, and where there are many hands [6].

42.6.0.en: What does he mean here by locking up, to keep the wicked wife from going out? Perhaps it means that the wicked woman here is one who practices sinful marital unfaithfulness or squanders his property foolishly. It seems from the next statement [7] that the wife is unfaithful with his property; so the locking up here is meant as watching over her so that she does not squander their property.

42.6.1.en: And if you deposit anything (of money), deposit it by number and weight, and record in writing whatever you take or give [7].

42.6.2.en: If doubt enters a man's mind that his wife is squandering his money or his produce or his possessions, it is better to record everything so that he does not let doubt take control of him.

42.6.3.en: And do not be ashamed to instruct the ignorant and the foolish, or the man advanced in years who condemns the young [1].

42.7.0.en: Then you will truly be instructed, and accepted before every man [8].

42.7.1.en: It seems that the statement here is directed to the leaders in the Jewish synagogues who are committed to teaching and guidance, even regarding the elders who mistreat the young; they must be guided so as to narrow the gap between the old generation and the new. On the other hand, it is fitting for us to realize that there is no man immune from error, even if he is an elder or a prophet. God sent to King David Nathan the prophet to urge him to repent (2 Sam 12).

42.7.2.en: There is no partiality with God. Although He had established David as prophet, king, and judge, and he had a glorious history of holy life, yet when he sinned he deserved correction. St. Irenaeus says: [God is no respecter of persons, therefore He imposes a fitting punishment on conduct that does not please Him. So it was in the case of David, who suffered persecution from Saul (1 Sam 18) for the sake of righteousness, and fled from King Saul and did not wish to take revenge on his enemy, and sang of the coming of Christ, and taught the nations wisdom, and did everything under the guidance of the Spirit, and God was pleased with him. But when his lust drove him to take Bathsheba the wife of Uriah, the Scripture says: "But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD." And He sent to him Nathan the prophet to point out to him his crime so that he might judge himself and condemn himself, and so obtain mercy and forgiveness from Christ[2],]

42.8.s.en: 2. The father's obligations toward his house

42.8.0.en: 9 A daughter is a hidden sleeplessness to her father, and a care that robs him of sleep, for fear of her remaining unmarried when she is grown, and of her being hated when she is married. 10 In her virginity, lest she be defiled, and be found with child in her father's house; and in marriage, lest she transgress against her husband, or be barren. 11 Keep a sure watch over the shameless daughter, lest she make thee a laughingstock to thine enemies, and a byword in the city, and a reproach among the people, and put thee to shame before the multitude.

42.8.1.en: There are no obligations for a father like his care for the upbringing of his sons and daughters. Society at that time was occupied with the marriage of daughters. And the responsibility of the household was to prepare the girl for a pure and successful married life.

42.8.2.en: Ben Sira had before him the first woman in the world, Eve, who brought shame upon her house. Therefore he presented to us some of the concerns of the good father toward his daughter, with love, wisdom, and fatherly firmness.

42.8.3.en: The daughter is a secret anxiety to her father[3], and his anxiety over her robs him of sleep.

42.8.4.en: Lest the time of marriage pass her by in her youth, and lest she be hated in her marriage [9]

42.8.5.en: v The enemy of holiness is always pressing upon the virgins and putting them in trouble, to make them prey when one of them staggers and falls. There are many treacherous people, and besides this they have a rebellious nature.

42.8.6.en: The (virgin) must prepare for a double battle: first she is attacked from without, and second she is corrupted from within[4].

42.9.0.en: St. John Chrysostom And in her virginity lest she be defiled or become pregnant while in her father's house, and of unfaithfulness if she has a husband, and of barrenness if she is married [10].

42.9.1.en: Daughters were a burden on the father, since three things occupied him: her marriage at the proper age, her purity and protection lest anyone assault her or seduce her, and the bearing of children.

42.10.0.en: Keep a close watch over the stubborn daughter, lest she make you a laughingstock to your enemies, a source of rumor in the city, of ill repute among the people, and a shame before the great multitude [11].

42.10.1.en: The talk here [9-11] reveals the anxiety of fathers regarding their responsibilities toward their daughters. If she is a young girl in her father's house, he fears that the age of marriage will pass her by and she will become a spinster. He also fears that someone may violate her, and she will become a shame to him. And if she marries, he fears that she will be unfaithful to her husband. And if she is faithful, he fears that she will be barren.

42.10.2.en: By the Incarnation of the Word of God from the holy Virgin St. Mary, all these fears passed away, for "there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28). And St. Mary surpassed not only all men but surpassed the heavenly orders.

42.11.0.en: 12 Gaze not upon the beauty of any, and sit not among women. 13 For from garments cometh the moth, and from the woman wickedness. 14 A man that doeth ill is better than a woman that doeth good, who bringeth shame and reproach.

42.11.1.en: Do not gaze at the beauty of any person, and do not sit among women [12].

42.11.2.en: He did not say: "Do not look at the beauty of any person," but he said "Do not gaze." For the man of God is holy in his looks, but if he is lax and gazes in looking, the grace of God abandons him.

42.12.0.en: For from garments comes the moth, and from woman the wickedness of a woman [13].

42.12.1.en: Garments that are not used for a long time are spoiled, as the eggs of the moth hidden in them hatch, and so human life is spoiled by the hidden evils in the soul such as wickedness and deceit.

42.13.0.en: The wickedness of a man is better than a woman who does what is good while bringing shame and reproach [14].

42.13.1.en: In many ancient societies there is a hidden contrast that is hard to perceive: ordinarily the man engrossed in his affairs does not practice his wickedness in secret and with deceit, but his words reveal what is within him, while the wicked woman sometimes is such that one cannot perceive what is in her inner intention. This contrast does not apply to every man or woman.

42.13.2.en: Some manuscripts have: "A dignified daughter is better than a son who has little shame[5]."

42.14.s.en: 4. The creation of the world glorifies God[6]

42.14.0.en: 15 I will remember the works of the Lord, and declare what I have seen. In the words of the Lord are his works. 16 The sun that giveth light looketh upon all things, and the work of the Lord is full of his glory. 17 Hath not the Lord made the saints to speak all his marvellous works, which the Lord the Almighty established, that the whole creation may be established in his glory? 18 He searched out the deep and the heart, and understood all crafty devices. 19 The Lord knew all knowledge, and looked upon the sign of the age, declaring the things that are past and the things to come, and revealing the traces of hidden things. 20 No thought escapeth him, neither is any word hidden from him. 21 He hath adorned the great works of his wisdom, and he is from everlasting to everlasting, and nothing hath been added, 22 neither is anything diminished, and he hath no need of counsel. 23 How desirable are all his works, and what is seen of them is as a spark. 24 All these live and remain for ever for every need, and all of them obey him. 25 All things are double, one against another, and he hath made nothing imperfect; 26 but the one establisheth the good of the other. And who shall be filled with beholding his glory?

42.14.1.en: In the second and third parts of this chapter Ben Sira laments the state of the father whose daughter brings upon him shame and disgrace before everyone through her stubbornness toward her husband or her impurity [9-11]. And the young man who enjoys the company of women with a spirit of recklessness and laxity [12-14] becomes like a garment eaten by the moth, and a plaything in the hand of a wicked woman who moves him toward shame and disgrace while he does not care! Now in this part [15-25] he sees the irrational creation moving through the laws of nature, and bearing witness by its movements and works to the glory of God, His wisdom, His providence, and His power.

42.14.2.en: The inanimate creation, which was not granted reason with its intelligence and abilities, nor the will to move it, works in exceeding harmony and order. The Apostle says: "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse" (Rom 1:20).

42.15.0.en: Creation, with the billions of creatures it contains, great and small, visible and invisible, was not brought into being scattered, but with an exact and wonderful order, into the secrets of whose precise laws the world is still searching up to this moment. Sirach says: "The Most High knows all knowledge, and looks upon the signs of the times [18].

42.15.1.en: These statements were in the mind of the Apostle Paul: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen" (Rom 11:33-36).

42.15.2.en: Ben Sira sees creation as the chariot of God's wisdom, offering it to every seeker of wisdom.

42.15.3.en: v "All his works are in faithfulness"; what does this mean? The heavens and their order you will find to be "a guide to faith," for they bear witness to their Maker. And if you see the order of the earth, it increases your faith in God. Yet it is not through ourselves, with our bodily eyes, that we believe in Him, but by the power of the mind we perceive the invisible through the evidence of the visible [7].

42.15.4.en: St. Basil the Great And now I will remember the works of the Lord and declare all His works that I see; by a word of the Lord His works were created, and all are subject to His will [15].

42.15.5.en: As Ben Sira speaks of God's works in nature, he mentions God's saying or word, for it is written in the Book of Genesis: "And God said, Let there be... and it was so..." (Gen 1:3).

42.15.6.en: St. Basil the Great shows that creation is the work of the Holy Trinity, so that when the divine command "Let there be..." was issued, it does not mean the issuing of sound waves in the air, but the issuing of the will of our God, with a divine mind; for creation was accomplished by the Word of God, "the Son." And when it is said that the Spirit was hovering, it does not mean that He made a movement in the air. Rather He played "an active part in creation." He is like a bird that broods an egg with its body, and by the warmth of its body offers a vital power that brings life.

42.15.7.en: v God created by His word animals of different kinds for our benefit, some of which we use as food and some in our service.

42.15.8.en: But man, God created him to be a witness to the works of God and one who gives thanks to Him for them.

42.15.9.en: This is what men must strive for, lest they die like the dumb animals without seeing or perceiving God and His works. Man must also know that God is able to do all things, and that no one can resist God the Almighty.

42.15.10.en: And just as God brought everything by His word from nothing into being according to His will, so (now) He makes everything for the salvation of mankind[8].

42.15.11.en: St. Anthony the Great The sun gives light and looks upon everything, and its work is full of the glory of the Lord [16].

42.15.12.en: As St. Basil the Great takes us on a delightful journey with the Creator, he offers us wonderful spiritual touches. We come into contact with the creativity of the Creator, not only to satisfy the needs of His beloved man, but in order to work in him, so that He may set up for him a beautiful, joyful world and a school that refines his conduct. We mention by way of example the following[9]:

42.15.13.en: a. As the sun gives light, so the saints in ancient times dispelled the darkness of ignorance[10].

42.15.14.en: b. As the moon waxes until it becomes full and then wanes, so the human destiny succeeds in virtue and fails in turn[11].

42.15.15.en: c. Some animals discover by instinct the coming seasons and prepare for them; so it is fitting for Christians to look forward to eternity and to hasten toward it[12].

42.15.16.en: d. Animals walk with bent backs, looking to the ground and to their bellies, but man was created with his head upward that he may care for heavenly things and not earthly ones[13].

42.15.17.en: The Lord did not enable His saints to describe all His wonders, which the Lord Almighty made, in order to establish the world in His glory [17].

42.15.18.en: None of the heavenly orders can declare the wonders of God that bear witness to His glory.

42.15.19.en: He searches the deep and the heart of man and understands their secrets, for the Most High possesses all knowledge, and looks upon the signs of the age [18].

42.15.20.en: He links the searching of the abyss, a bottomless, with the heart, for as no one can reach the depths of the immeasurable abyss, so the heart of man contains within it a world whose secrets no one can know but the Most High.

42.15.21.en: St. Basil begins his homilies on the "six days of creation" with the work of God the Creator for the sake of man, His beloved, and at the close of his homilies (especially Homily 9:6 and Homily 11:14) he affirms the necessity of setting out on a journey to the depths of the soul, so that the believer may discover the microcosm, far more wonderful than the outer world. The saint affirms that getting to know the invisible heaven is easier than man's getting to know his own depths. The inner man is a special and precious world into which one must enter with the Spirit of the Holy God, so that we may know ourselves and grow in the knowledge of God.

42.16.0.en: He declares the past and the future and reveals the traces of hidden things [19].

42.17.0.en: No thought escapes Him, and not one word is hidden from Him [20].

42.18.0.en: He adorned His great works with His wisdom, and He is the One who exists from eternity to eternity; nothing can be added to Him, nor anything taken from Him, and He has no need of anyone to be His counselor [21].

42.18.1.en: The main idea around which the homilies of St. Basil the Great on the days of creation revolve is that the true beauty of creation, with all its systems that seem extremely complex, and its wonderful creativity, can be perceived and realized by returning to the eternal, invisible world that awaits us and welcomes us, as we long for it and look forward to it through the wonderful love of the Creator for man[14]. Therefore, when Rousseau devoted a chapter to the Hexaemeron, he called it: "A return to the ancient homeland," quoting this from (Homily 6:1).

42.19.0.en: How precious are all His works, how they sparkle to the sight [22].

42.19.1.en: The stories of creation as recorded by the philosophers conflicted and contradicted one another, but what Moses the prophet recorded in the Book of Genesis is the fruit of an encounter with God, and his talk comes to kindle our hearts not to know how creation was accomplished, but how we meet the Creator and enjoy the sight of Him, and enter with Him into a shared love!

42.19.2.en: The world has a beginning and surely has an end, "for the fashion of this world passeth away" (1 Cor 7:31). So while we receive this beautiful gift from the hand of the Creator, it is fitting that our hearts be attached to the eternal Creator, not to the passing creation.

42.19.3.en: Moses the prophet affirms: "In the beginning God created," for the world did not bring itself into being, but is the making and creativity of the Creator.

42.20.0.en: All these live and remain forever for every need, and all of them are obedient [23].

42.21.0.en: All things are made in pairs, one the counterpart of the other, and He has made nothing imperfect [24].

42.21.1.en: St. Evagrius of Pontus sees that prayer also is accomplished in two ways, by action and by contemplation[15].

42.22.0.en: Each one of them strengthens the goodness of the other, so who can have enough of beholding His glory? [25]

42.23.s.en: Let me walk according to Your good pleasure, O my Creator!

42.23.0.en: v My soul rejoices in Your Law and in entering into a covenant with You!

42.23.1.en: It lifts me up, so that I gladly give up even my temporal rights.

42.23.2.en: My heart will not turn aside from the faith, whatever the temptation.

42.23.3.en: I and the members of my household walk with propriety, for You are our leader in life.

42.23.4.en: v Who is my only daughter whose marriage and chastity and bearing of holy children I care for!

42.23.5.en: She is my soul, whose dowry You paid on the cross. She dwells in the Church, the holy house of marriage.

42.23.6.en: And her children are the fruit of the Holy Spirit!

42.23.7.en: v For my sake You created the wonderful universe, through which I touch Your surpassing love for me.

42.23.8.en: You created the sun for my sake, so that my soul may be illumined by You.

42.23.9.en: Your care for all creation is surpassing, how much more what You are preparing for my eternity?

42.23.10.en: I long to see You in Your eternal glory!
